title: Midgut Malrotation -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Midgut malrotation is a congenital disruption of normal intestinal rotation and fixation during early gestation, resulting in abnormal bowel positioning and a narrowed mesenteric base, which predisposes patients to volvulus and obstruction at any age. Normal midgut development involves herniation into the umbilical cord, a 270-degree counterclockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric artery, and mesenteric fixation to the retroperitoneum. Failure or arrest at any stage produces a spectrum of rotational anomalies, including nonrotation, incomplete rotation, reverse rotation, and anomalous mesenteric fixation. This course reviews the clinical presentation of midgut malrotation, which ranges from acute neonatal volvulus with bilious vomiting and rapid systemic compromise to chronic, nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms in older children and adults. Diagnostic evaluation, which relies on high clinical suspicion, imaging modalities, and definitive management centering on the Ladd procedure, which derotates volvulus and often includes appendectomy to prevent future complications, is also discussed.

content: This activity reviews the acute and subtle clinical features of midgut malrotation across age groups and interprofessional management for optimal patient outcomes. title: Midgut Malrotation -- Introduction
content: Midgut malrotation is a congenital abnormality of intestinal position and fixation resulting from interruption of the normal 270-degree counterclockwise rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) during early gestation. This disordered rotation leaves the small bowel and colon in atypical locations and, more importantly, creates a narrow mesenteric base that predisposes to midgut volvulus and intestinal obstruction at any age. [1]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Introduction
content: During normal development, the rapidly elongating midgut herniates into the umbilical cord around the fifth week of gestation and undergoes an initial 90 degree counterclockwise rotation around the SMA while extra-abdominal. As the bowel returns to the abdominal cavity between approximately 10 and 12 weeks of gestation, the bowel completes a further 180 degree counterclockwise turn (total 270 degrees), positioning the duodenojejunal junction to the left of the spine at the level of the pylorus and the cecum in the right lower quadrant; subsequent mesenteric fixation to the retroperitoneum establishes a broad-based mesentery that stabilizes the midgut and prevents torsion. Failure, arrest, or reversal of rotation at different stages produces a spectrum of rotational anomalies collectively referred to as malrotation. [2] Types of midgut malrotation include: Nonrotation Incomplete rotation Reverse rotation Anomalous fixation of the mesentery [3]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Introduction
content: The clinical spectrum ranges from catastrophic neonatal volvulus to chronic or intermittent symptoms and entirely asymptomatic malrotation. In neonates and young infants, the typical presentation is abrupt onset of bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and systemic deterioration due to midgut volvulus, which constitutes a surgical emergency because rapid vascular compromise can lead to extensive bowel necrosis within hours. Beyond infancy, patients may present with recurrent colicky abdominal pain, postprandial bloating, intermittent vomiting, or failure to thrive, and diagnostic delay is common as symptoms are often nonspecific. A substantial subset of individuals remain asymptomatic, with malrotation discovered incidentally during imaging or operations for unrelated conditions; nonetheless, the presence of a narrow mesenteric pedicle means that even these “incidental” cases carry a lifelong risk of sudden volvulus. [4]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Introduction
content: Rotational anomalies frequently coexist with other congenital defects, and recognition of these patterns is important for comprehensive care. Cardiac malformations and chromosomal syndromes, particularly trisomy 21, are overrepresented among infants with duodenal obstruction and malrotation. Malrotation is also highly prevalent in heterotaxy (situs ambiguus) syndromes, occurring in 60% to 100% of patients, and is accompanied by complex cardiac lesions, splenic abnormalities (asplenia or polysplenia), anomalous systemic and portal venous anatomy, and other foregut and midgut anomalies. Additional gastrointestinal associations include duodenal atresia or stenosis, jejunoileal atresia, annular pancreas, Meckel diverticulum, and intestinal duplications, many of which may require simultaneous or staged surgical correction. These patterns underscore that intestinal malrotation is often part of a broader developmental disturbance of laterality and foregut–midgut morphogenesis rather than an isolated anatomic curiosity. [5] [6]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Introduction
content: Diagnosis relies on a high index of suspicion supported by characteristic imaging findings. An upper gastrointestinal contrast series remains the reference standard, demonstrating an aberrant position of the duodenojejunal junction to the right of the spine or failure of the duodenum to cross the midline, with a corkscrew configuration of the proximal small bowel in volvulus. In contemporary paediatric practice, abdominal ultrasound is increasingly used as a first-line modality, with abnormal SMA to superior mesenteric vein (SMV) relationships and the “whirlpool sign” of swirling mesenteric vessels serving as key indicators of malrotation and active volvulus, respectively. Cross-sectional imaging with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is especially valuable in older children and adults, clarifying anatomy, demonstrating vascular compromise, and identifying associated anomalies. [7] [8]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Introduction
content: Definitive management of midgut malrotation is surgical. The Ladd procedure, comprising counterclockwise derotation of any volvulus, division of Ladd’s bands, broadening of the mesenteric base, placement of small bowel on the right and colon on the left, and usually an appendectomy, does not restore normal rotation but aims to eliminate duodenal obstruction and reduce the risk of recurrent volvulus. Outcomes are excellent when diagnosis is timely, and bowel remains viable; however, mortality and long-term morbidity increase substantially in the presence of extensive ischemia, prematurity, severe cardiac disease, or complex syndromic associations.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Etiology
content: Etiology of midgut malrotation remains only partially understood and appears multifactorial, involving abnormal embryonic rotation/fixation, perturbations of left–right patterning, and a heterogeneous set of genetic and syndromic associations rather than a single uniform cause. The core etiologic event is failure of the midgut to complete its normal sequence of herniation, 270° counterclockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric artery, and subsequent mesenteric fixation during early gestation. Arrest, delay, or misdirection at any stage leads to a shortened mesenteric root, malposition of the duodenojejunal junction and cecum, and persistence of abnormal peritoneal attachments (Ladd bands), all of which create a predisposition to duodenal obstruction and volvulus. In this sense, malrotation represents a primary disorder of intestinal morphogenesis and mesenteric fixation rather than an acquired condition. [9] [10] [11]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Etiology
content: Most cases are sporadic, but familial clustering and twin concordance suggest a genetic contribution in a subset of patients. Copy-number variants and single-gene defects have been described in association with intestinal malrotation, including mutations in transcription factors involved in mesenteric left–right asymmetry (eg, NODAL-regulated pathways and FOXF1) and rare chromosomal rearrangements (for example, 16q24.1 or ring chromosome 4) that combine malrotation with other foregut, pulmonary, and vertebral anomalies. Malrotation is also a recognised component of broader syndromic diagnoses, particularly heterotaxy syndromes. In this disruption, of ciliary function and left–right axis specification genes leads to discordant visceral situs, complex congenital heart disease, splenic abnormalities, and a very high prevalence of rotational abnormalities. A genome-wide association study identified a locus on chromosome 17p13 associated with the condition, implicating several genes involved in embryonic gut development, including PITPNA , TRARG1 , and INPP5K . Additional associations have been reported with chromosomal aneuploidies (including trisomy 21) and multisystem malformation syndromes; however, no single inheritance pattern (autosomal dominant, recessive, or X-linked) accounts for the majority of cases. [12] [13] [14]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Etiology
content: Perinatal characteristics appear to modify risk and presentation rather than directly cause malrotation. Prematurity and low birth weight are overrepresented among infants with symptomatic malrotation and volvulus, likely reflecting global disturbances of fetal growth and organogenesis rather than a specific environmental insult to the midgut. Epidemiological series have noted variation in reported incidence across populations, but robust links to particular maternal variables (eg, age, parity, or nutritional status) remain unproven after adjustment for their effects on prematurity and low birth weight. Overall, current evidence supports a model in which malrotation arises from intrinsic errors in embryonic rotation and fixation on a background of genetic susceptibility and disordered laterality, with perinatal factors influencing the timing and severity of clinical expression rather than serving as primary causes. [15]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Epidemiology
content: Epidemiologic data on midgut malrotation reflect its status as a relatively uncommon but likely under-recognized congenital anomaly, with a broad clinical spectrum from asymptomatic rotational variants to catastrophic neonatal volvulus.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Epidemiology
content: Reported birth incidence varies because many individuals remain asymptomatic and are never imaged. Surgical and population-based series suggest that malrotation occurs in roughly 1 in 200 to 500 live births radiologically, but only about 1 in 6,000 live births present clinically in infancy. A Hawaiian registry study reported an incidence of approximately 2.9 per 10,000 live births and fetal deaths, with a high proportion (over 90%) of affected infants having at least 1 additional major congenital anomaly, underscoring the syndromic burden in this cohort. Autopsy and imaging data indicate that the true prevalence of rotational anomalies in the general population is higher than the clinically apparent incidence, as many cases are incidental findings without symptoms. [11] [4]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Epidemiology
content: Malrotation has traditionally been regarded as a disease of infancy because most symptomatic cases present early in life. Approximately 30% of children with clinically significant malrotation present within the first month, about 60% by the end of the first year, and more than 75% by 5 years of age, most often with bilious vomiting and features of intestinal obstruction or volvulus. Nevertheless, contemporary series demonstrate that malrotation can first manifest in adolescence or adulthood, usually with chronic or intermittent abdominal symptoms rather than fulminant volvulus; adult-onset disease accounts for only about 0.2% to 0.5% of all malrotation cases, and among these adults, only a minority (around 15%) present with acute midgut volvulus. [16] [8] [17]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Epidemiology
content: Rotational anomalies frequently coexist with other congenital malformations, particularly cardiac, gastrointestinal, and laterality defects. Large pediatric series document congenital heart disease, heterotaxy, abdominal wall defects (eg, omphalocele), congenital diaphragmatic hernia, oesophageal and intestinal atresias, biliary atresia, and complex anorectal malformations (including VACTERL spectrum) in a substantial proportion of patients with malrotation, often exceeding 30% to 40% in tertiary referral cohorts. Heterotaxy syndromes are especially notable, with intestinal malrotation reported in 60% to 100% of such patients and contributing significantly to their gastrointestinal morbidity. Most series show a modest male predominance, with male infants affected approximately twice as often as females. However, sex ratios vary somewhat between populations and between radiologic versus surgically treated cohorts. [18] [19] [6]

content: The history and physical examination in intestinal malrotation are strongly age and acuity-dependent, ranging from fulminant neonatal volvulus to subtle, chronic symptoms in older patients.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features in Infants
content: In the first months of life, the classic presentation is that of acute bowel obstruction, most often due to midgut volvulus. Parents typically report a sudden onset of vomiting that is classically bilious (green or yellow-green), although early episodes may be nonbilious if the obstruction is proximal or intermittent. Any bilious emesis in an infant younger than 1 year is considered an ominous sign and should prompt urgent evaluation for obstructive pathology, including malrotation with or without volvulus.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features in Infants
content: On physical examination, early findings may be surprisingly subtle. The abdomen can be soft and only mildly distended, particularly when the obstruction is high in the duodenum or proximal jejunum. As ischemia progresses, signs of systemic compromise emerge: tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cool extremities, and hypotension reflecting hypovolemia and evolving shock. Local signs—abdominal tenderness, guarding, erythema of the abdominal wall, or overt peritonitis—tend to be late and indicate advanced volvulus with inflammation or perforation. Hematochezia or bloody gastric aspirate suggests mucosal infarction and possible transmural necrosis of the midgut. [20] [21] [22]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features in Children
content: Beyond early infancy, the presentation often becomes less dramatic and more protean. Children may have recurrent or intermittent episodes of crampy periumbilical or upper abdominal pain, sometimes postprandial, that can last minutes to hours and resolve spontaneously, reflecting intermittent volvulus or partial obstruction from Ladd bands. Vomiting is common but not invariably bilious, and some patients are labelled as having “reflux,” “colic,” or functional abdominal pain before malrotation is recognised. Failure to thrive, early satiety, chronic bloating, and altered bowel habits (including constipation or loose stools) may accompany these symptoms in long-standing cases.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features in Children
content: Physical examination between acute episodes may be normal or show only nonspecific findings such as mild epigastric tenderness or distension. During an acute obstructive event, abdominal distension, tympany, focal or diffuse tenderness, and occasionally visible peristalsis can be detected. Persistent tachycardia, fever, localized guarding, and rebound should raise concern for evolving ischemia or perforation and mandate urgent imaging and surgical consultation.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features in Adults
content: In adults, malrotation is uncommon and typically presents with chronic, nonspecific symptoms rather than catastrophic volvulus, which occurs in only a minority of cases. Many report long histories of intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, bloating, or episodic vomiting, often triggered by meals and sometimes associated with weight loss or food avoidance. A subset presents with acute small-bowel obstruction or midgut volvulus, characterised by sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to initial examination, repeated bilious or feculent vomiting, and rapid hemodynamic deterioration if diagnosis is delayed.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features in Adults
content: The adult physical examination can be misleadingly bland early on, with mild distension and diffuse tenderness but no clear peritonism. As obstruction progresses, high-pitched or absent bowel sounds, marked distension, localized peritoneal signs, and systemic toxicity (tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria) develop, mirroring the progression seen in infants. Because history and examination are often nonspecific outside the neonatal period, a high index of suspicion is essential, especially when recurrent or unexplained obstructive-type symptoms occur in a patient with no prior abdominal surgery. [4] [22]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Evaluation
content: Evaluation of suspected intestinal malrotation requires rapid assessment of hemodynamic stability, targeted laboratory studies, and definitive imaging to confirm diagnosis and guide management. In unstable patients with bilious vomiting and signs of peritonitis or shock, immediate surgical consultation and operative intervention supersede extensive imaging. However, stable patients warrant a systematic approach incorporating laboratory data and radiographic confirmation.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Studies
content: Initial laboratory evaluation provides critical prognostic information and guides preoperative optimization. A complete blood count often reveals leukocytosis (>15,000/μL) or leukopenia signaling systemic inflammation or sepsis, while thrombocytopenia (<100,000/μL) suggests consumptive coagulopathy and thrombocytosis (>500,000/μL) reflects the acute-phase response. Hemoconcentration (elevated hematocrit) indicates hypovolemia from third-spacing, whereas anemia suggests mucosal hemorrhage from ischemia.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Studies
content: Blood gas analysis with serum lactate is essential for assessing bowel viability. Metabolic acidosis (pH <7.35, base excess <-4) and lactate levels less than 2 mmol/L strongly suggest mesenteric ischemia, with levels higher than 4 mmol/L correlating with bowel necrosis and poor outcomes. A comprehensive metabolic panel typically demonstrates hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric losses (Cl <90 mEq/L, K <3.5 mEq/L, HCO3 >30 mEq/L), while late ischemia may show hyperkalemia (>5.5 mEq/L) from cellular destruction. Coagulation studies (PT/PTT, fibrinogen) assess for disseminated intravascular coagulation in advanced cases, and type-and-screen preparation anticipates potential massive transfusion.

A comprehensive metabolic panel typically demonstrates hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric losses (Cl <90 mEq/L, K <3.5 mEq/L, HCO3 >30 mEq/L), while late ischemia may show hyperkalemia (>5.5 mEq/L) from cellular destruction. Coagulation studies (PT/PTT, fibrinogen) assess for disseminated intravascular coagulation in advanced cases, and type-and-screen preparation anticipates potential massive transfusion.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Evaluation -- Abdominal radiography
content: Abdominal radiography serves as an initial screening tool but has limited diagnostic value for malrotation specifically (sensitivity 69%, specificity 57%). Films may appear normal early or demonstrate nonspecific small-bowel distension with air-fluid levels. A "double-bubble" sign (air-filled stomach and proximal duodenum, with distal gas paucity) suggests high duodenal obstruction due to Ladd bands or volvulus. When pneumoperitoneum is suspected, left lateral decubitus or cross-table lateral views improve sensitivity over supine films. [23]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Evaluation -- Upper gastrointestinal series
content: In hemodynamically stable patients, upper gastrointestinal contrast study remains the reference standard for malrotation diagnosis (sensitivity 93%, specificity 77%, accuracy 86%). Normal anatomy demonstrates a duodenal C-loop that smoothly crosses the midline, with the duodenojejunal junction positioned left of the spine at the pyloric level. Malrotation appears as a duodenojejunal junction right of midline (>1 cm right of spine), failure of duodenal crossing, or spiral "corkscrew" configuration of proximal jejunum indicating volvulus. A beak-like distal duodenal cutoff suggests complete obstruction. Small-bowel follow-through can clarify distal obstruction when needed, though it delays diagnosis in acute volvulus. [24]

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Treatment / Management -- Recommended Management Approaches
content: In any patient, especially an infant with bilious emesis and suspected obstruction, immediate priorities are airway protection, nasogastric or orogastric decompression, intravenous fluid resuscitation, and broad-spectrum antibiotics, followed by urgent surgical consultation. Signs of peritonitis, sepsis, or hemodynamic instability mandate rapid transfer to the operating room for exploration, often without delay for complete imaging, because midgut volvulus can progress to transmural necrosis within hours. Hemodynamically stable patients undergo confirmatory imaging (usually upper gastrointestinal series or ultrasound), but a high index of suspicion should still prompt early operative management when volvulus is likely.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Intervention
content: An appendectomy is routinely performed during the Ladd procedure for 2 main reasons. First, due to the altered positioning of the bowel, the appendix often ends up in the left upper quadrant, which could lead to diagnostic confusion in future cases of appendicitis. Second, the appendiceal artery may be compromised during the division of Ladd bands, making removal of the appendix a preventive measure against future complications. However, recent series and a 2023 systematic review note a growing minority who deliberately preserve the appendix, particularly in patients where it may be needed later for a MACE/ACE conduit or urinary diversion, arguing that modern imaging, documentation, and follow-up make missed appendicitis unlikely and that the Ladd procedure without appendectomy appears safe on medium-term follow-up. When midgut volvulus is present, many surgeons defer a full Ladd rearrangement and anastomoses until after the patient has been resuscitated and bowel viability clarified at second look, particularly in unstable neonates with extensive ischemia. title: Midgut Malrotation -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Intervention
content: The Ladd procedure can be performed via open laparotomy or laparoscopy, and both approaches follow the same operative principles. Open surgery (typically via right upper quadrant transverse or midline incision) provides rapid, wide exposure and remains preferred in unstable patients, those with grossly distended bowel, or when extensive resection is anticipated. Laparoscopic Ladd procedures in stable infants and older patients are associated with less postoperative pain, a shorter hospital stay, and a quicker return of bowel function, and large series and recent comparative studies suggest similar rates of postoperative volvulus, with a potential reduction in adhesive small-bowel obstruction. Concerns persist that laparoscopy may provide less complete mesenteric broadening and fewer protective adhesions, which could theoretically increase the risk of recurrence, but contemporary data do not show a clear difference in volvulus recurrence when procedures are performed by experienced surgeons. title: Midgut Malrotation -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Intervention
content: For symptomatic patients without acute volvulus, eg, those with chronic abdominal pain, intermittent obstruction, or failure to thrive, the elective Ladd procedure is generally recommended, as symptoms typically improve and the risk of catastrophic volvulus is reduced. Management of incidentally discovered, asymptomatic malrotation remains controversial: many pediatric surgeons advocate prophylactic Ladd procedure in otherwise healthy children because the lifetime risk of volvulus has been estimated at 15% to 20%, whereas others favour individualized decision-making based on age, comorbidities, and family preference. In heterotaxy or complex congenital heart disease, some centres delay elective Ladd until after cardiac stabilization or reserve surgery for symptomatic patients, balancing volvulus risk against perioperative cardiac morbidity.

Children who have undergone extensive bowel resection need nutritional support and long-term follow-up for short-bowel syndrome and growth failure.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Neonatal bilious vomiting and bowel obstruction Duodenal atresia : Polyhydramnios antenatally, "double-bubble" sign on x-ray, complete duodenal cutoff on upper gastrointestinal proximal to ampulla of Vater. Jejunoileal atresia : Failure to pass meconium for >48 hours, bilious vomiting with abdominal distension, multiple dilated loops, and microcolon on contrast enema. Meconium ileus : Cystic fibrosis association (90%), calcifications/soap-bubble sign on x-ray, microcolon with filling defects on contrast enema. Hirschsprung disease : Delayed meconium passage for more than 24 to 48 hours, explosive stool after rectal exam, transition zone on contrast enema with absent ganglia on biopsy. Annular pancreas : Associated with Down syndrome, characterized by duodenal narrowing encircled by pancreatic tissue on upper gastrointestinal series, and may coexist with malrotation. Small left colon syndrome : Maternal diabetes history, transient functional obstruction, narrow left colon with normal right colon on contrast enema.

title: Midgut Malrotation -- Prognosis
content: Patients undergoing a timely Ladd procedure for intestinal malrotation without midgut volvulus, bowel necrosis, prematurity, or complex congenital anomalies enjoy excellent long-term prognosis, with most achieving normal growth and resolution of symptoms. [44] Surgical mortality ranges from 3% to 9% overall, but escalates significantly with the following adverse factors: Midgut volvulus increases mortality to 5% to 25%, particularly when diagnosis is delayed beyond 6 hours or extensive necrosis requires massive resection. Prematurity and low birth weight independently double mortality risk. Associated cardiac anomalies (present in 27%-33%) and heterotaxy syndromes further elevate perioperative morbidity through hemodynamic instability and multisystem involvement. Modern series report neonatal volvulus mortality as low as 3%-7% when managed at high-volume centres with rapid imaging-to-surgery pathways. [45]

content: Postoperative morbidity affects 30% to 60% of patients, primarily prolonged ileus (most common), wound complications, and central line infections. Adhesive small-bowel obstruction occurs in 10% to 20% of cases, often requiring reoperation, though laparoscopic approaches may reduce this risk. Recurrent midgut volvulus, despite adequate Ladd procedure, complicates 2% to 8% of cases and can present months to years later, emphasizing the need for vigilant follow-up in patients with persistent symptoms. Short-bowel syndrome develops in 10% to 30% of volvulus cases requiring more than 50% small-bowel resection, with TPN dependence, bacterial overgrowth, and failure to thrive as long-term sequelae. content: Nurses are often the first to detect subtle deterioration, rising lactate, increasing abdominal distension, new tenderness, or changes in perfusion, and their vigilance, timely escalation, and use of structured early-warning tools directly influence survival. They coordinate nasogastric decompression, fluid resuscitation, antibiotic delivery, and preoperative optimization, while providing continuous bedside communication to surgeons and anesthesiologists about evolving hemodynamics and pain. Radiologists contribute by prioritizing imaging studies in critically ill children, using standardized reporting language (eg, “whirlpool sign consistent with midgut volvulus”) that clearly communicates urgency and reduces interpretive ambiguity. Pharmacists enhance safety by verifying weight-based dosing of broad-spectrum antibiotics, analgesics, and vasoactive agents, monitoring for nephrotoxicity or drug interactions, and supporting parenteral nutrition regimens in patients with short bowel or prolonged ileus. Dietitians, speech therapists, and intestinal rehabilitation teams are crucial in long-term management of children with significant resections, designing individualized feeding plans, monitoring micronutrient status, and helping families transition from TPN to enteral nutrition when feasible.
